"Sumit, the audit is Monday," said Darshan, the department manager. "I need the supplier agreement dated last March."

"It was signed in June, sir."

"I know. Change the date. It's a formality."

Sumit stood still, then pulled out the chair. "Give me a minute. If someone checks that record later, what does it say? That the agreement existed in March. And it didn't."

"It's only paperwork."

"The policy says records show what really happened. If I sign a false one, it's my name on it. And I would know."

Darshan rubbed his forehead. "You're making this hard."

"I'm not saying no to the audit, sir. I'm saying I can't write a false date."

qa.q: When was the supplier agreement actually signed?
How does Sumit feel about signing the false date?
qa.a: Sumit feels uneasy but determined, because even if nobody else found out, Sumit would know the record was false.

qa.q: What could Sumit offer Darshan next, and why would that help?
qa.a: Sumit could offer to prepare a note that explains the June signing and get it ready before Monday, because it answers the audit need without a false date.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel under the audit deadline?
qa.a: Darshan is likely stressed and pressed for time, which explains why the request is called a formality and the refusal is heard as making things hard.

grounding: An employee asked to backdate a document asks what a false record would mean and recalls policy and personal integrity.

I'm Pranav, eight months into my first job as an analyst. Last Tuesday my manager, Akash, stopped at my desk and said, 'The vendor approval form for the Mehta account, just date it the 3rd, not the 17th. Audit's tomorrow. It's a formality.'
My first feeling was panic. He's my manager. Everyone likes him. I nearly just did it.
Instead I went to the pantry and asked myself one question: if an auditor reads this form, what will it say that isn't true? It would say we approved the vendor before any work began. We didn't. The form would be a false record, and my name would be on it as preparer.
Then I remembered the code-of-conduct training from my first week: never alter dates on records. And something simpler: I don't want to be someone who signs things that aren't true.
Once I'd named it, the fog cleared. I went back and told Akash I couldn't change the date, but I could write a note explaining the delay. He sighed, then said, 'Fine. Write the note.'

qa.q: What date did Akash want on the form?
How did Pranav feel when Akash first asked?
qa.a: Pranav felt a rush of panic, tempted to comply because Akash was the manager and well liked.

qa.q: What else could Pranav do if Akash had insisted?
qa.a: Write down what was asked and when, and check with a trusted senior or HR how such requests are handled.

qa.q: How might Akash see Pranav's answer?
qa.a: Akash may be irritated at first but accepts the note, perhaps realising the backdating put them both at risk.

grounding: Shows a junior analyst asked to backdate a form asking what a false record would mean, and recalling policy and personal integrity.

Mentor's note, graduate programme, 11 August. Lakshmi, senior auditor.
Keerthana came to me this afternoon, visibly shaken. Her team manager had asked her to change the date on a stock-count sheet so it would look as if the count happened before the quarter closed. The client audit is on Friday.
I didn't tell her what to do. I asked her what the sheet would claim if she changed it. She thought for a moment. 'That we counted on the 30th. We counted on the 4th.' Then, more slowly: 'So it would be a false record. And company policy says we never alter dates. I signed that policy in my first week.'
She sat back. 'It's not a grey area, is it? It just felt grey because he's my boss.'
She said she felt steadier once it had a name. She plans to tell her manager she can't change the date, and to offer a note explaining the late count. I've asked her to update me tomorrow.

qa.q: When did the stock count actually happen?
How did Keerthana feel once the principle had a name?
qa.a: Steadier and clearer, after arriving visibly shaken by the pressure.

qa.q: What could Keerthana do if the manager insists?
qa.a: Keep a written note of the request and take it to Lakshmi, HR or the ethics channel, rather than giving in.

qa.q: How does the conversation look to Lakshmi, who wrote the note?
qa.a: Lakshmi asks questions instead of giving answers, and watches Keerthana reach the principle herself.

grounding: Shows a junior employee asked to backdate a record working out what the false date would claim and naming the policy and value at stake.
